title: Server Side APIs
summary: Calling third-party APIs from Django with Python's requests library, keeping API keys in .env files with python-dotenv, OAuth1 for APIs that need it, formatting results for your front end, and mocking API calls in unit tests. Step-by-step guide arrives when the lecture is published.
goal: Call a third-party API from a Django view with its key loaded from a .env file, and test it with a mocked request.

steps.title: Make a request from Python
steps.detail: requests is the standard Python library for calling other APIs. Try it in your practice venv.
steps.code:
cd ~/Desktop/django-practice && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install requests python-dotenv
python -c "import requests; print(requests.get('https://api.github.com').status_code)"

steps.title: Review where your Netflix keys live
steps.detail: Netflix keeps keys in assignments/week-02/netflix/.env.local, and .gitignore lists `.env` and `.env.local`. Anything with a VITE_ prefix gets shipped to the browser, so only public keys belong there. A Django server keeps truly secret keys in its own .env, loaded with python-dotenv, and the browser never sees them. Module 3 (3rd-party APIs, Oct 19–22) covers the same idea with serverless functions.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain why a secret API key belongs in Django's .env and never in a VITE_ variable.

steps.title: Read about mocking
steps.detail: Read the `patch` section of Python's unittest.mock docs. Mocking means your tests never call the real API, so they stay fast and free.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain what `@patch('requests.get')` swaps out during a test.

concepts.meaning: Someone else's service your server calls for data, like weather or movies.
